security_audit.summary: All 383 static findings are false positives involving Markdown backticks, language identifiers, relative module imports, or the mops documentation link. Three semantic risks affect example applications: unrestricted timer scheduling, unpublished post visibility, and anonymous callers sharing todo ownership. No evidence found of malicious execution, credential exfiltration, or audit-directed prompt injection.

remediation.issue: The timer example exposes scheduling and cancellation without authorization and overwrites existing timer handles.
remediation.suggestion: Restrict timer controls to authorized callers, keep a transient optional handle, and cancel an existing timer before scheduling another.

remediation.issue: The public blog query returns unpublished posts, including their content and author details.
remediation.suggestion: Filter public results by published status and provide a separate authenticated query for an author's drafts.

remediation.issue: The todo example accepts anonymous callers as owners, giving unrelated anonymous clients the same ownership identity.
remediation.suggestion: Reject anonymous callers before creating, reading, or modifying personal records, and test access from unrelated anonymous clients.

semantic_findings.description: Public startPeriodicCleanup schedules recurring work without authorization and overwrites timerId without cancelling earlier timers. Any caller can accumulate background jobs or stop cleanup.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: Both public controls lack caller checks, and each start replaces the handle without cancelling the previous recurring timer. This enables resource abuse if deployed.

semantic_findings.description: New posts start unpublished, but getAllPosts returns every post through toView, including content and author details. This bypasses draft visibility if publication controls access.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The public query has no publication filter or caller restriction, and the projection includes content. Confidentiality impact depends on the application's intended draft policy.

content.value_statement: Outdated Motoko examples can cause compiler errors and unsuitable backend designs. This skill provides modern language references, modular actor patterns, and mops dependency workflows.
actual_capabilities: Guide backend organization across types, domain modules, API mixins, and an actor composition root.
Reference core collection signatures, contextual dot notation, implicit comparison functions, and numeric conversions.
Explain query, update, and composite query constraints, including shared types at API boundaries.
Provide option handling, typed error results, record mutation, and iterator patterns.
Guide mops dependency installation, synchronization, integrity recovery, compile checks, and final builds.
Explain persistent and transient state conventions and when separate migration guidance is required.
limitations: Targets moc 1.11.2 or later, mops 3.x, and core 2.6.0 or later; older projects may require adaptation.
State changes and canister upgrades require separately referenced migration skills that are not included here.
Compiler verification requires an installed Motoko toolchain and project configuration; these documents do not execute tests themselves.
Examples require security hardening, including timer authorization, draft visibility controls, and rejection of anonymous personal-record access.

use_cases.title: Build a First Motoko Service
use_cases.description: Use modern syntax and shared API types to organize a small backend into domain modules, mixins, and actor state.

use_cases.title: Repair Backend Compile Errors
use_cases.description: Compare failing collection calls, imports, and conversions against the supplied signatures and diagnostic guidance.

use_cases.title: Align APIs With Client Bindings
use_cases.description: Define immutable response views and caller-scoped endpoints before using generated backend bindings in a client application.

prompt_templates.title: Explain Modern Motoko
prompt_templates.prompt: Explain query versus update functions and shared response types for a simple Motoko todo service. Use this skill's supported toolchain assumptions.

prompt_templates.title: Design a Modular Backend
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a Motoko backend for [domain]. Separate types, domain helpers, API mixins, and actor state. Identify authorization rules and migration prerequisites.

prompt_templates.title: Fix a Compiler Diagnostic
prompt_templates.prompt: Resolve [compiler diagnostic] in [source excerpt]. Verify relevant core signatures, preserve behavior, and propose focused mops checks without changing platform-managed flags.

prompt_templates.title: Implement Caller-Scoped Services
prompt_templates.prompt: Implement [service] using injected state, immutable views, and typed errors. Reject anonymous personal-record access. Bound privileged operations and include negative authorization tests.

output_examples.input: How should I organize a blog canister with mutable users and posts?
output: Keep entity types in the schema module and domain methods in separate user and post modules.
Inject only required state into each API mixin, and keep the actor as the composition root.
Return immutable views. Restrict public lists to published posts and authorize access to drafts.
Initialize durable state through the configured migration chain before running compiler checks.

output_examples.input: A Nat-keyed map operation reports that the compiler cannot determine compare. What should I check?
output: Import the core Nat module in the file performing the map operation.
Map operations resolve their implicit comparator from the imported key-type module.
Verify the operation signature, then rerun the mops check after fixing the import.

output_examples.input: Which return type should a booking endpoint use for expected caller errors?
output: Return a typed result with an immutable success view and an error variant.
Use separate error tags for authorization failures, unknown rooms, and occupied slots.
Reserve traps for broken invariants and options for normal absence.

best_practices: Verify toolchain versions and uncertain core APIs against the supplied references before implementing changes.
Define backend authorization and visibility policies, then test anonymous, unauthorized, and repeated privileged calls.
Use mops for dependency changes, iterate with compile checks, and build only after checks pass.
anti_patterns: Copying example services into production without reviewing authentication, publication rules, and recurring resource costs.
Guessing JavaScript-style collection methods or mixing deprecated base APIs with modern core conventions.
Changing persistent actor state without migration guidance or manually editing dependency lockfiles.

faq.question: Does it include core API signatures?
faq.answer: Yes. It supplies signatures for collections, text, principals, options, results, timers, and other core modules.

faq.question: Does it handle canister migrations by itself?
faq.answer: No. It explains state conventions and directs migration work to separate skills that are not included in this package.

faq.question: Does reading the skill run commands?
faq.answer: No. The package contains Markdown guidance. Applying its mops workflows can install dependencies, modify project files, and produce build artifacts.
